newsitem.title: DUBAI: Iran wargames were warning to Gulf Arabs-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Iran wargames were warning to Gulf Arabs-analysts.

text.p: Iranian wargames in the Gulf and a renewed threat about the Strait of Hormuz were intended as a warning to Arab oil states in the region not to act like U.S. satellites, Gulf-based analysts and diplomats said on Sunday.
The four-day exercises by the Revolutionary Guards, trained over the past two years as the Islamic republic's rapid reaction force, and Basij militia volunteers, were defensive, they said.
"Two things drove them: The Iranians were saying 'We want to show that we're here and we're a force to be reckoned with'," a Western Iran-watcher based in the Gulf said.
"This has both an internal resonance and, in the current climate, an external one: 'If you do start something you're going to get stuck'.
"Second, they were saying: 'We are prudently preparing our ability to cope with any aggression,' which is what everybody has been talking about very publicly for the past six months."

Gulf-based analysts said perceived chances of a flashpoint were higher now than for some time because the two camps -- Iran and the West -- were shouting at each other. But at the same time chances of hostilities breaking out by mistake through a local misinterpretation or misunderstanding were lower.
"In terms of what everyone is talking about -- al-Khobar -- there isn't anything around at the moment which would justify American action," one analyst said.

A U.S. State Department official said in Washington last month that the United States had not concluded Iran was behind the deadly truck bombing of a U.S. military housing complex at al-Khobar in Saudi Arabia but would take action if it did.

Although the threat about Iran's power to close the Strait of Hormuz, the strategic channel between Iran's southern coast and the tip of the Arabian peninsula, was not new analysts said its timing was significant.

The commander of the Revolutionary Guards, Major-General Mohsen Rezaei, said after last month's amphibious exercises by naval, air and ground forces: "We can keep the Strait of Hormuz open...but if we want to, we shall close this strait to anyone who is an obstacle to security in the region and keep it open for our friends and the Moslems."
A Gulf analyst called the remark "pretty heavy-handed".
About 15 million barrels of oil -- half the world's exports -- pass through the 55 KM (35 mile) wide strait each day on the way to markets in Asia, Europe and the United States.

Iranian officials had repeatedly said they had no intentions of threatening the world's supply of oil and a closure of the Strait would shut off Iran's own oil exports, which accounts for 90 percent of its foreign currency earnings.

The world's largest producer, Saudi Arabia, could switch a significant part of its oil exports to Red Sea terminals in case of the closure of the Strait. Iraq, which has the world's second largest oil reserves, could use a pipeline through Turkey.
The renewed threat was part of the propaganda effect of the wargames, said another analyst who monitors Iran.
"Some of that is designed for local government consumption.

"'Do take it seriously. We are the regional power. Don't play the Americans' games for them because if you do you are going to suffer locally. We can close the Strait of Hormuz. We can stir up problems in your countries. You are in range.'
"Those sorts of messages are conveyed in order to discourage certain Gulf countries from, as the Iranians would see it, behaving like an American satellite," the analyst added.

The exercises, watched by Iran's supreme leader and armed forces commander-in-chief Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, included test launches of a variety of missiles, some with sufficient range to reach the Arab side of the Gulf.

But a U.S. Navy official said: "It was best described as static displays of equipment and naval and air reviews. The down to earth term would be parades of aircraft and ships in very simple field manoeuvres and a small firepower demonstration. There was no real use of any advanced tactics."
"It was truly an exercise in politico-military diplomacy."
The United States has about 20 warships and auxiliary support vessels in the Gulf to protect oil supplies to the West.
